one_liner: Header-only C++26 work-stealing thread pool with about 3x to 7x lower scheduling overhead than Taskflow and BS::thread_pool on tiny tasks.
what_it_does: A general-purpose task pool: execute() for fire-and-forget noexcept callables, submit() returning task<T> whose get() yields std::expected<T, std::exception_ptr>, fork_join(f, g), when_all/map/and_then combinators, and parallel_for/parallel_map plus chunked variants. basic_pool takes feature tags (priority, cancellable, trace, worker_cap<N>, queue_cap<G, L>), and an optional stdexec (P2300) scheduler adapter exists. The interface is its own, so it does not drop in for Taskflow or BS::thread_pool.
how_it_is_fast: Each worker has a Chase-Lev work-stealing deque. External submissions go to a bounded global MPMC ring with an overflow chain, and task nodes come from per-thread node caches, so the hot path avoids allocation. Submit/complete accounting is sharded per thread on separate cache lines. Idle workers spin for a time budget (64 us by default) before sleeping on a futex-style atomic wait, and a wake wakes one sleeper only when no spinner is active. fork_join is work-first: it enqueues one branch and runs the other inline.
when_to_use: Many sub-microsecond tasks where per-task scheduling cost dominates, such as fire-and-forget event fan-out (8.39 M tasks/s vs Taskflow 1.24 in the author's run).
Latency-sensitive submit-then-wait round trips on a pool kept warm: P50 0.44 us vs 2.66 us (Taskflow) when workers are still spinning.
Recursive divide-and-conquer with tiny leaves, where it roughly matches oneTBB (27.39 vs 25.69 M leaves/s) and beats Taskflow about 3x.
New C++26 codebases on GCC 16.2+ that want std::expected-based error handling, no exceptions escaping fire-and-forget tasks, and optional priorities or cancellation.
when_not_to_use: Anything not on GCC 16.2+ with -std=c++26 -fcontracts: Clang, MSVC and older GCC are not supported (it uses contracts and <inplace_vector>).
Compute-bound chunks: the author's own fixed-workload test at 4 threads has nexus at 3.26 ms vs Taskflow 2.59 ms (slower).
Sparse or bursty service traffic on shared machines: the 64 us spin budget keeps idle workers burning cores, and the latency win depends on it (lower spin_budget for such pools).
Task-graph dependencies (Taskflow's DAG model) or production use that needs maturity: the project is about one month old (first commit 2026-08-27), has 1 star and its docs are in Chinese only.

integration.dependencies: none (Threads; optional oneTBB, Taskflow and stdexec for benchmarks and tests)
integration.min_toolchain: C++26, GCC 16.2+, CMake 3.28+ with Ninja for the CMake build; -fcontracts is required at compile and link time
integration.platforms: Not documented beyond the author's Linux x86-64 run (i7-12650H); uses standard atomics and std::jthread only
integration.thread_safety: submit/execute are safe from any thread, including workers (nested submits go to the local deque); pool wait()/shutdown() must not be called from inside a pool task (deadlock, contract-checked in Debug)

gotchas: execute() and the f branch of fork_join require noexcept callables; submit() routes exceptions into the expected result channel, and a successful result can be taken only once.
fork_join does not join: both branches stay in flight after it returns, and you sync with pool wait() or your own counter, as the benchmark does with an atomic leaf count.

The constructor may throw on thread creation; pool::try_create() is the no-throw path. The default queue_cap is 65536 global / 256 local, and full rings spill into an overflow chain rather than rejecting work.

The benchmarks time empty tasks that bump one shared atomic counter, so they measure scheduler overhead, not useful throughput; 8 producers plus 8 workers on a 10-core/16-thread laptop also oversubscribe it.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick nexus over dpuyda/scheduling or ThunderBolt-HT when you also want futures, combinators and priorities on top of low-overhead stealing; pick Fork Union or citor for parallel-for dispatch on large many-core machines, and oneTBB when you need a mature, portable runtime (nexus's fork-join lead over it is only about 7%).
verified_claims_summary: The author ran benchmarks/bench.cpp on an Intel i7-12650H with 8 workers, GCC 16.2.1, CMake Release (-O3, no -march), taking the best of three runs on 2026-09-30. nexus reached 8.39 M tasks/s single-producer fire-and-forget vs Taskflow 1.24 and BS::thread_pool 0.40, 28.40 vs 8.62 vs 1.23 M leaves/s on depth-18 fork-join, and P50/P99 round trip 0.44/0.87 us vs 2.66/7.44 and 3.75/6.01. The same run against oneTBB was much closer (fork-join 27.39 vs 25.69, 8-producer 7.31 vs 6.53), and on a compute-bound workload at 4 threads nexus was slower than Taskflow.
status_note: Active (34 commits from 2026-08-27 to 2026-09-30) and MIT-licensed header-only code that is easy to vendor, but it is very young, has a single author and needs a bleeding-edge GCC 16.2.
